Adequacy of a support against the saturated graph

Source: R/wald.R
mc_test_adequacy.Rd

Tests whether the edges a support omits can all be zero at once. The saturated graph is refitted on the same residuals, complete in the undirected layer and complete along the same ordering in the directed one, and the parameters of the omitted edges are tested jointly by mc_wald_graph under the covariance of that saturated fit (an adequacy check of a selected structure). With \(E_{\max}\) the set of all pairs of responses and \(\hat E\) the edges of the support, the null hypothesis is \(H_0:\theta_e=0\) for every \(e\in E_{\max}\setminus\hat E\), against the saturated graph, and the statistic is the Wald statistic of mc_wald_graph with the contrast that selects those \(|E_{\max}|-|\hat E|\) parameters.

Usage

mc_test_adequacy(
  fit,
  type = c("sandwich", "model", "two_stage"),
  cluster = NULL,
  small_sample = FALSE,
  method = c("auto", "shortcut", "full")
)

Arguments

fit

an object of class "mcglm_graph" whose support omits at least one edge; the saturated graph is refitted from its residuals and must converge.

type

the covariance: "sandwich" (default), "model" or "two_stage", as in mc_vcov_graph.

cluster

optional vector with one identifier per observational row. With type = "sandwich" or "two_stage", the contributions are summed within clusters before the variability is formed, which is the form to use when the unit of dependence is not the row of the data matrix. It must have no missing value and at least two distinct values; the default NULL takes the rows as the units. It is refused with type = "model".

small_sample

logical, default FALSE; multiply the clustered variability by \(G/(G-1)\), with \(G\) the number of clusters. It has no effect without cluster and is refused with type = "model".

method

for type = "two_stage", the route of the correction: "shortcut", "full", or "auto" (default). "auto" takes the full form when it is available and either a response has a variance function other than "constant" or the fitted DAG has an immorality; in every other case it takes the shortcut when it applies and the full form when it does not. The full form rebuilds the first stage and is slower. It has no meaning for the other two types.

Value

An object of class "htest" as in mc_wald_graph, whose degrees of freedom are the number of omitted edges, with the extra components omitted (a two-column matrix i, j of the omitted pairs of responses), n_saturated (the number of edges of the saturated graph) and descriptive_after_selection, always TRUE.

A diagnostic, not a test at nominal level

If the omitted edges were fixed before looking at the data, the statistic would be referred to a chi-squared distribution with as many degrees of freedom as edges omitted. When the support was chosen by a search on the same data, that reference is only the one of a fixed support: the result is descriptive, with no claim of nominal level after selection. A large p-value says that the zeros of the support are compatible with the residual covariance; a small one says that at least one omitted edge carries partial association. The returned object records this in descriptive_after_selection.

See also

mc_wald_graph, mc_test_independence and mc_graph_stepwise.

Other inference on the graph layer: mc_test_independence(), mc_two_stage_available(), mc_vcov_graph(), mc_wald_graph()

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1); n <- 400
K <- diag(4) * 2; K[1, 2] <- K[2, 1] <- -0.7; K[3, 4] <- K[4, 3] <- -0.7
Y <- matrix(rnorm(n * 4), n) %*% chol(solve(K))
d <- data.frame(y1 = Y[, 1], y2 = Y[, 2], y3 = Y[, 3], y4 = Y[, 4],
                x = rnorm(n))
f <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x, y4 ~ x), data = d)
#> Automatic initial values selected.
sel <- mc_graph_stepwise(f, criterion = "bic", trace = FALSE)
mc_test_adequacy(sel$fit)
#> 
#> 	Wald test of adequacy against the saturated graph (sandwich covariance;
#> 	descriptive after selection)
#> 
#> data:  4 of 6 edges omitted from a GGM layer
#> X-squared = 3.3534, df = 4, p-value = 0.5005
#> sample estimates:
#> [1] -0.007881532  0.017153068  0.035587530 -0.115230131
#> 
# }
